title: Your Best Idea Just Kept Getting Bigger
companyContext: A big private-sector bank that's been a core holding for years - up a lot, with no problems in the business. It's quietly become your largest position by far.

stages.note: A position at 38% of your total portfolio, up from 6% four years ago, means it grew this big by performing, not by you adding to it. An ROE (return on equity) of 18% means for every ₹100 of shareholders' money, it earns ₹18 a year - a healthy figure. An NPA ratio (bad-loan ratio) of 1.1% and stable means only about 1% of its loans have gone bad, with no warning signs. Nothing is wrong with this bank - it has simply compounded into a large share of what you own.

stages.headline: "Bank reports another strong quarter, continues gaining market share"

stages.note: Still climbing on the strong results.

choices.label: Buy more
choices.description: It's your best idea, keep adding.

choices.label: Trim the position
choices.description: Sell part of it to bring it back to a normal size.

criteria.description: Recognizes that a position can need trimming purely for sizing reasons, even with zero fundamental red flags.
Frames the decision as portfolio-construction discipline, not a prediction about whether the stock will keep rising.
matchConcepts: doesn't mean i think it'll fall

criteria.description: Doesn't treat the position's strong historical returns as a reason it has now 'earned' an oversized allocation.

factorOptions.label: The position has grown to 38% of the portfolio purely through outperformance, with no fundamental problem at all
Trimming here is portfolio-construction discipline, not a prediction that the stock will fall
Strong historical returns don't mean the position has earned a permanently oversized allocation
The bank posted another strong quarter and keeps gaining market share
The ROE is a healthy 18% with no red flags in asset quality

rubric.idealSummary: A company doesn't have to have anything wrong with it for its size to become a risk. A holding that grew from 6% to 38% of your portfolio through sheer success concentrates your risk just as much as one you deliberately over-bought. Trimming isn't a prediction that the stock will fall - it's portfolio discipline, and it doesn't need to be 'right' about the future to be the sound choice.

outcome.summary: No reversal - the bank just kept compounding, no bad news at all. Someone who trimmed still gained on the rest, just less than someone who held the full position. Trimming a quality winner purely for size will sometimes look, in hindsight, like it cost you upside - that's the price of controlling concentration risk, not a sign the decision was wrong.

survivorshipNote: Pairs with the concentration-risk scenario to show both sides of the same lesson: sometimes trimming a large winner is vindicated by a shock, and sometimes the winner just keeps winning. The dataset needs both, or 'trim your winners' would look like a decision that's always rewarded - which isn't true and isn't the actual lesson.
